Physical Education (PE) inc. Swimming
Intent
At The Phoenix Federation, we believe that high-quality Physical Education is essential to supporting pupils’ physical development, mental wellbeing and overall health. Our PE curriculum is ambitious for all pupils and is designed to inspire children to develop a lifelong love of physical activity while building the knowledge, skills and confidence needed to lead healthy, active lives.
We aim to provide every pupil with opportunities to succeed and excel in a broad range of physical activities and sports. Through carefully planned, progressive learning experiences, pupils develop fundamental movement skills, teamwork, resilience, leadership, cooperation, and sportsmanship.
Our curriculum promotes physical competence, personal achievement and positive attitudes towards physical activity. We want children to understand the importance of staying active, making healthy choices and recognising the positive impact that exercise has on both physical and mental wellbeing.
PE also supports the development of our Federation values. We encourage pupils to be aspirational in striving to improve, brave in taking on new challenges, compassionate towards teammates and competitors, determined when developing new skills and enlightened through an understanding of healthy lifestyles and personal wellbeing.
We are committed to ensuring that all pupils, regardless of their starting point, are supported and challenged to achieve their potential and develop the confidence to participate fully in sport and physical activity both now and in the future.
Implementation
Physical Education is taught throughout the Federation using the PE Hub Scheme of Learning, which provides a carefully sequenced and progressive curriculum from Early Years through to Year 6.
All pupils receive a minimum of two high-quality PE lessons each week, delivered by class teachers and supported by qualified sports coaches. Lessons are designed to build knowledge, skills and confidence over time, ensuring pupils develop increasing competence across a broad range of physical activities.
The curriculum is organised around three key strands:
Physically Competent, Physically Active
Pupils develop fundamental movement skills, coordination, balance, agility and control, building the foundations for successful participation in a wide range of sports and physical activities.
Tactics and Strategies
Pupils learn how to apply skills within competitive and cooperative situations, developing decision-making, problem-solving, creativity and teamwork. They learn how tactics influence performance and how to adapt strategies within games and sporting contexts.
I Can, I Want To, I Will
Pupils develop confidence, resilience, determination and a positive mindset towards physical activity. They learn to evaluate their own performance, set personal goals and recognise the value of effort, perseverance and self-improvement.
Across the curriculum, pupils experience a broad range of activities, including:
Learning is carefully sequenced so that knowledge and skills build progressively from one year group to the next. For example, children in the Early Years develop fundamental movement skills through manipulating, coordinating and controlling their bodies. These foundations are then built upon throughout Key Stage 1 and Key Stage 2 as pupils apply their skills within increasingly complex games, sports and competitive situations.
Assessment for learning is embedded throughout lessons. Teachers use observation, questioning, pupil self-assessment, peer assessment and end-of-unit assessments to monitor progress, identify misconceptions and inform future teaching. This ensures pupils secure key knowledge and skills over time and understand how to improve their performance.
Dance
Gymnastics
Athletics
Invasion games
Net games
Striking and fielding games
Outdoor and adventurous activities
Fitness activities
Swimming
Swimming is a vital life skill and forms an important part of our PE curriculum. Pupils in Years 3, 4 and 5 attend swimming lessons at Wavelengths Leisure Centre where they are taught to:
Perform safe self-rescue in different water-based situations.
Develop confidence and water safety awareness.
PE Enrichment and Competitive Sport
We enrich our curriculum through a wide range of sporting opportunities that encourage participation, enjoyment, competition and personal achievement.
Pupils regularly take part in inter-school, local and cross-Federation competitions, festivals and sporting events. These include participation in cricket tournaments, basketball competitions, SEND sports festivals, and a range of local sporting events, enabling pupils to apply their skills in competitive and inclusive environments while demonstrating teamwork, resilience, determination, and sportsmanship.
Our strong partnership with Millwall Football Club provides pupils with additional coaching, enrichment activities and regular opportunities to participate in tournaments and sporting festivals throughout the year. These experiences allow pupils to develop their skills alongside children from other schools, build confidence, broaden their horizons and experience the positive benefits of organised sport.
We also host and participate in annual events including Sports Week and Sports Day, held at venues such as Goldsmiths, University of London and other local community facilities. These events celebrate participation, achievement and personal bests whilst promoting healthy competition and strengthening the sense of community across the Federation.
Where possible, pupils are given opportunities to meet and learn from experienced coaches, athletes and sporting role models who inspire them to develop ambition, perseverance and a lifelong commitment to physical activity.
Impact
The impact of our PE curriculum is evident in pupils who are increasingly confident, active and motivated participants in physical activity and sport.
By the time pupils leave The Phoenix Federation, they:
Pupils benefit from a wealth of competitive and enrichment opportunities that enable them to apply their learning in a variety of contexts. Through participation in tournaments, sporting festivals and partnership events with organisations such as Millwall Football Club, pupils develop confidence, leadership skills, teamwork and resilience. They learn how to compete positively, celebrate success, manage disappointment and demonstrate respect for others, preparing them well for future participation in sport and wider life experiences.
Through participation in both mainstream and SEND sporting competitions, pupils develop confidence, self-belief and a sense of belonging, ensuring that every child has the opportunity to experience success, represent their school and develop a lifelong enjoyment of physical activity.
Assessment information demonstrates that pupils build upon prior learning and develop increasing proficiency across the curriculum. Through regular opportunities to practise, apply and refine their skills, pupils become more confident and capable learners. Most importantly, pupils leave The Phoenix Federation with positive attitudes towards physical activity and an understanding of the importance of maintaining healthy, active lifestyles. They are equipped with the knowledge, skills and confidence to continue participating in sport and physical activity beyond primary school and throughout their lives.
Compete with honesty, respect, fairness and integrity.
Subject Statement
“At The Phoenix Federation, we believe that every child should experience the joy, challenge and success that Physical Education can bring. Our PE curriculum is designed to build confidence, resilience and teamwork whilst developing the physical skills needed for lifelong participation in sport and physical activity. Through high-quality teaching, competitive sport, partnerships with organisations such as Millwall Community Trust, and enrichment opportunities including cricket, basketball and inter-school tournaments, we ensure every pupil has the opportunity to thrive. We aim to develop healthy, active and confident young people who understand the value of determination, respect, sportsmanship and striving to achieve their personal best.”

Relationships and Health Education (PSHE and RSE)
Intent
At the Phoenix Federation, we believe that Personal, Social, Health and Economic Education (PSHE) is a fundamental part of every child’s education and personal development. We are committed to nurturing confident, resilient, respectful and responsible young people who are well prepared for life both now and in the future.
Our PSHE curriculum is underpinned by our Federation values of being Aspirational, Brave, Compassionate, Determined and Enlightened. Through carefully planned learning experiences, we aim to equip children with the knowledge, understanding, attitudes and practical skills they need to lead safe, healthy, fulfilling and purposeful lives.
We recognise that children are growing up in an increasingly complex and diverse world. Our curriculum supports pupils in developing a strong sense of identity, self-worth and belonging, whilst fostering respect, empathy and understanding towards others. We celebrate individuality and diversity, ensuring that children value the unique qualities that make them who they are whilst recognising the positive contribution they can make to their communities.
We aim to develop children’s emotional literacy, wellbeing and resilience so that they are able to manage challenges, build positive relationships, make informed decisions and seek support when needed. Through our PSHE curriculum, pupils develop the knowledge and confidence to stay safe, maintain positive mental and physical health, understand healthy relationships and become active, responsible citizens.
Through exposure to a broad range of experiences, perspectives and opportunities, we encourage children to become ambitious about their futures, develop an understanding of the wider world and recognise the many pathways available to them throughout their lives.
Implementation
Across the Phoenix Federation, we follow the PSHE Association Programme of Study, ensuring a comprehensive, ambitious and progressive curriculum that develops the whole child. Learning is organised through carefully sequenced, age-appropriate units which build knowledge, skills and understanding over time.
The curriculum is structured around three core themes:
Our curriculum follows a spiral approach, enabling pupils to revisit and deepen their understanding of key concepts throughout their primary education. Prior learning is regularly revisited and built upon, helping children to make connections between new learning and existing knowledge.
Teachers adapt learning to reflect the needs, experiences and backgrounds of their pupils, ensuring that all children can access and engage fully with the curriculum. Through discussion, enquiry, reflection and real-life contexts, children are encouraged to think critically, develop self-awareness and express their views respectfully.
A key feature of our PSHE curriculum is our growing work around the Zones of Regulation. Through these bespoke units, children develop a greater understanding of emotions, self-regulation and wellbeing. Pupils learn to recognise emotional states, understand the physical and emotional signs associated with different feelings and identify personal triggers. They develop a personalised toolkit of strategies that support emotional regulation, enabling them to respond to challenges in positive and productive ways.
Mindfulness opportunities are embedded throughout the curriculum to develop self-awareness, concentration, emotional regulation and resilience. These approaches support children’s mental health and wellbeing and help create calm, purposeful learning environments.
Recognising the importance of technology in children’s lives, digital literacy and online safety are integral to our curriculum. Pupils learn how to navigate the online world safely and responsibly, critically evaluate information, understand digital relationships and become respectful and responsible digital citizens.
As part of our commitment to raising aspirations, pupils in upper Key Stage 2 participate in learning focused on future pathways, careers and aspirations. Through careers events, visitors, enrichment opportunities and discussions about the world of work, children begin to understand how their education can open doors to future opportunities and ambitions.
PSHE is further enriched through assemblies, themed weeks, pupil leadership opportunities, educational visits, charitable initiatives, community engagement and everyday interactions across school life. These experiences help children apply their learning in meaningful contexts and strengthen their understanding of what it means to be an active member of society.
Assessment is ongoing and informs future teaching. Teachers use discussion, questioning, reflection activities and pupil voice to assess understanding, identify misconceptions and respond to emerging needs. The impact of learning is reviewed regularly to ensure pupils develop the knowledge, skills and confidence intended by the curriculum.
Health and Wellbeing
Relationships, including Relationships and Sex Education (RSE)
Living in the Wider World
Impact
By the time pupils leave the Phoenix Federation, they will:
Through PSHE, we aim for every child to leave the Phoenix Federation as a confident, compassionate and responsible individual, equipped with the knowledge, skills and values needed to thrive in school, in their communities and in the wider world.

Religious Education (RE)
Intent
At Phoenix Federation, we aspire for our children to become thoughtful and reflective theologians, developing a deep understanding of a range of religious and non-religious worldviews and the role they play in shaping individuals, communities and society.
Our Religious Education curriculum encourages pupils to explore life’s big questions and develop their understanding of beliefs, values, identity, belonging and meaning. Through engaging with Christianity, other major world religions and a range of worldviews, pupils are encouraged to consider questions such as:
We want pupils to develop secure knowledge of religious traditions and beliefs whilst acquiring the skills to question, discuss, reflect, analyse, interpret and evaluate. Through their learning, pupils develop empathy, respect and an appreciation of the diverse communities that make up modern Britain and the wider world.
Our curriculum supports pupils’ spiritual, moral, social and cultural development, enabling them to reflect on their own beliefs and values whilst respecting the beliefs and experiences of others.
What do people believe and why?
What gives life meaning and purpose?
How do beliefs influence actions and choices?
What does it mean to belong?
How should people live together?
Implementation
Religious Education is taught as a distinct subject in accordance with the Lewisham Agreed Syllabus for Religious Education. Learning is carefully sequenced to build knowledge and understanding progressively throughout each pupil’s primary journey.
Each unit begins with an enquiry question that encourages pupils to think critically, explore different perspectives and engage deeply with the focus of learning. Throughout each unit, pupils develop both substantive knowledge about religions and worldviews and disciplinary knowledge, learning how to think, question and reason as theologians.
As pupils move through the curriculum, they revisit and deepen their understanding of key concepts, beliefs, practices and traditions. This ensures that knowledge is retained and built upon over time, enabling pupils to make meaningful connections between religions and worldviews.
Christianity forms the largest part of the curriculum in line with the Lewisham Agreed Syllabus. In addition, pupils study Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism, ensuring a broad understanding of the major world faiths represented both nationally and globally.
Through engaging lessons, pupils:
Retrieval practice is embedded throughout the curriculum to help pupils remember and build upon previous learning. Teachers use a range of formative assessment strategies, including questioning, discussion, reflective activities, quizzes and exit tickets, to assess understanding and identify misconceptions. Exit tickets provide regular opportunities for pupils to recall key knowledge, reflect on their learning and articulate their understanding of important concepts, beliefs and worldviews, enabling teachers to adapt future learning where necessary.
Learning is enriched through visits to places of worship, visits from faith representatives, community links, assemblies and the celebration of religious festivals. These first-hand experiences deepen pupils’ understanding of different beliefs, cultures and communities while strengthening their appreciation of diversity within modern Britain and the wider world.
Explore sacred texts, stories and religious teachings.
Investigate religious beliefs, practices and traditions.
Ask and answer challenging questions.
Discuss ethical and moral issues.
Impact
The impact of our Religious Education curriculum is evident in the knowledge, confidence, curiosity and open-mindedness demonstrated by our pupils.
By the time they leave The Phoenix Federation, pupils have developed a secure understanding of a range of religious and non-religious worldviews and can discuss beliefs, values and practices with increasing confidence, sensitivity and respect.
Assessment information gathered through discussion, written work, reflection activities, quizzes and exit tickets demonstrates that pupils are able to recall, connect and apply their learning with increasing confidence and accuracy. As a result, pupils develop a deeper understanding of religious beliefs, practices, values and worldviews, enabling them to engage thoughtfully with complex questions about faith, identity, morality and human experience.
Pupils leave The Phoenix Federation as reflective, respectful and informed young people who possess the knowledge, skills and understanding needed to continue their study of religion and worldviews. They are prepared to engage thoughtfully with different beliefs and perspectives and contribute positively to their local, national and global communities.

“At The Phoenix Federation, we believe that Religious Education plays a vital role in helping children understand themselves, others and the world around them. Through learning about a range of religions and worldviews, pupils develop knowledge, curiosity and respect whilst exploring life’s most important questions. We encourage children to think critically, reflect deeply and engage thoughtfully with different beliefs and perspectives. Our aim is to develop confident, compassionate and open-minded learners who value diversity and are prepared to flourish in an increasingly interconnected world.”

Science
Intent – What do we want our children to learn?
At the Phoenix Federation, we believe that science is an important part of every child’s education. Science helps children to understand the world around them, ask questions, solve problems and make informed decisions about their lives and their future.
Our ambition is for every child to see themselves as a scientist. We want pupils to be curious, confident and enthusiastic about science and to understand how science influences everyday life and the wider world.
Our science curriculum is ambitious, inclusive and carefully sequenced from the Early Years through Key Stage 1 and Key Stage 2. Learning builds progressively on what pupils already know so that knowledge, scientific vocabulary and enquiry skills become increasingly sophisticated as children move through the school.
In the Early Years, children begin by exploring and making sense of the natural world through observation, questioning and first-hand experiences. In Key Stage 1, pupils develop their curiosity by observing closely, asking simple questions, identifying and classifying, carrying out simple tests and recording what they notice. In Lower Key Stage 2, pupils build on these foundations by asking increasingly relevant questions, choosing appropriate enquiries, making careful measurements, recording data and drawing conclusions. By Upper Key Stage 2, pupils are expected to plan enquiries with greater independence, consider variables, take increasingly accurate measurements, analyse results, use evidence to support conclusions and evaluate their findings.
This progressive approach ensures that pupils are well prepared for the next stage of their science education.
Our curriculum follows the National Curriculum for Science and develops both:
Working scientifically is embedded throughout the curriculum and is taught alongside scientific knowledge rather than as a separate subject. Children experience the different types of scientific enquiry, including observing over time, identifying and classifying, pattern seeking, comparative and fair testing, and researching using reliable secondary sources.
We place a strong emphasis on scientific vocabulary, reading, writing and oracy. Pupils are taught the vocabulary they need to explain their thinking accurately, discuss scientific ideas, challenge misconceptions and communicate conclusions confidently.
We also aim to develop pupils’ science capital. Children encounter scientists, engineers and STEM professionals from a wide variety of backgrounds, including people from our local community where possible. We deliberately introduce pupils to diverse scientists, including individuals whose contributions to scientific discovery have historically been less well known. This helps pupils understand that science belongs to everyone and opens their eyes to the wide range of careers connected to STEM.
Above all, we want children to leave the Phoenix Federation believing:
“Science is relevant to my life, I can be successful in science, and science could be part of my future.”
Implementation – How do we teach science?
Our science curriculum is planned carefully so that children know more, remember more and can do more over time.
Each year group’s curriculum identifies the important knowledge, vocabulary and scientific skills pupils need to learn. Teachers make explicit links to prior learning and revisit important concepts so that pupils can connect new knowledge to what they already understand.
Progression is deliberately planned across the Federation. Concepts are revisited at increasing levels of complexity. For example, children’s early observations of plants, animals and seasonal change provide foundations for later learning about habitats, life cycles, adaptation, inheritance and evolution. Similarly, early exploration of materials develops progressively into more sophisticated understanding of properties, states of matter and changes in materials.
High-quality teaching
Teachers create positive learning environments in which children are encouraged to be curious, ask questions, make predictions and learn from their observations.
Lessons are designed to be purposeful and engaging and include a balance of:
Practical work is carefully chosen because of what it helps pupils learn, rather than simply to make lessons enjoyable. Children are taught how to use scientific equipment appropriately and safely and how to collect increasingly accurate and meaningful evidence.
explicit teaching of important scientific knowledge;
teacher modelling and explanation;
practical investigations and first-hand experiences;
opportunities to ask and answer scientific questions;
discussion using accurate scientific vocabulary;
recording, presenting and interpreting findings;
retrieval and revisiting of previous learning; and
Working scientifically
Working scientifically is woven throughout science teaching. As pupils progress through the school, expectations increase from supported exploration towards greater independence. Children progressively learn to:
EYFSobserve, explore, notice similarities and differences, talk about change, ask questions and describe what they experience.
Key Stage 1ask simple questions, observe closely, identify and classify, carry out simple tests, gather information and record observations.
Lower Key Stage 2ask relevant questions, select different types of enquiry, set up simple comparative and fair tests, take measurements, gather and present data and use evidence to draw conclusions.
Upper Key Stage 2plan different types of enquiry, identify and control variables where appropriate, use equipment with increasing accuracy and precision, record more complex data, make predictions, explain results, evaluate evidence and identify further questions.
Vocabulary and communication
Scientific vocabulary is planned progressively so that children develop an increasingly precise scientific language.
Teachers model vocabulary explicitly and provide regular opportunities for pupils to use scientific terminology when speaking and writing. Children are encouraged to explain how they know, not simply provide an answer.
This strengthens scientific understanding while also supporting pupils’ wider development in reading, writing and spoken language.
Assessment
Assessment is an integral part of science teaching.
Teachers regularly check what pupils know and understand through questioning, discussion, observation of practical work, pupil explanations, retrieval activities and review of recorded work.
Assessment is purposeful and proportionate. It helps teachers to:
Teachers revisit important knowledge to strengthen pupils’ long-term memory rather than relying on one-off assessments at the end of a topic.
identify what pupils have remembered;
recognise misconceptions quickly;
adapt teaching where necessary;
Inclusion
We have high expectations for all pupils.
Science is planned and adapted so that pupils with SEND, disadvantaged pupils and pupils who may experience other barriers to learning can access the same ambitious curriculum alongside their peers.
Teachers use appropriate scaffolding, resources, vocabulary support, practical experiences and reasonable adjustments while maintaining high expectations for what pupils can achieve.
Enrichment and science capital
We raise the profile of science beyond individual lessons through enrichment opportunities such as science events, clubs, visitors, STEM ambassadors, educational visits and links with the wider community where appropriate.
These experiences help pupils understand how classroom science connects with everyday life, further education and future careers.
Leadership and monitoring
The Science Lead has a clear understanding of the strengths and priorities for science across the Federation and works alongside senior leaders and teachers to maintain high expectations and consistency.
The quality of the science curriculum is monitored through a range of appropriate activities, which may include:
Findings from monitoring are used to celebrate strengths, identify priorities and continually improve teaching, resources and curriculum provision.
Senior leaders and governors maintain appropriate oversight of science so that they understand how effectively the curriculum is being implemented and the difference it is making to pupils.
discussions with pupils;
review of pupils’ work;
lesson visits and learning walks;
curriculum and planning reviews;
assessment information;
discussions with teachers; and
professional development and staff feedback.
Impact – How do we know our science curriculum is successful?
The impact of our science curriculum can be seen in what pupils know, remember, understand and can do.
We want pupils to make strong progress from their individual starting points and to build secure scientific knowledge and skills year by year.
We evaluate the impact of our curriculum through teachers’ assessment, pupils’ work, discussions with pupils, observation of learning, curriculum monitoring and pupils’ ability to recall and apply previous learning.
Successful science education at the Phoenix Federation means that pupils:
confidently use increasingly sophisticated scientific vocabulary;
collect, present and interpret scientific evidence;
demonstrate curiosity, resilience, collaboration and independence;
By the time pupils leave the Phoenix Federation…

Modern Foreign Languages
Subject Statement
“At Oak Gardens Primary School, we believe that language learning opens doors to new cultures, experiences and opportunities. Our Spanish curriculum is designed to inspire curiosity, build confidence and celebrate the rich linguistic diversity of our school community. We want every child to see themselves as a successful language learner, developing the skills to communicate, explore new perspectives and engage with the wider world. Through learning Spanish, pupils not only acquire valuable language skills but also gain an appreciation of the cultures, traditions and communities that make our world such a diverse and exciting place.”
Intent
At Oak Gardens Primary School, we aspire for every child to leave Key Stage 2 as a confident, curious and capable language learner with a genuine appreciation of different languages, cultures and communities.
As part of the Phoenix Federation, we recognise and celebrate the rich linguistic diversity of our school community. Many of our children speak English as an additional language and bring a wealth of cultural and linguistic experiences to school. We value and celebrate these experiences and seek to foster a culture where all languages and cultures are respected.
Spanish has been carefully selected as our modern foreign language because it reflects the rich cultural and linguistic diversity of our community. Many of our pupils and families have connections to Spanish-speaking countries, including the Dominican Republic, Colombia and other parts of the Spanish-speaking world. Through learning Spanish, pupils are encouraged to celebrate and value both their own cultural heritage and that of others, fostering respect, understanding and curiosity about the wider world.
Our ambitious curriculum develops secure foundations in listening, speaking, reading and writing. Through carefully sequenced learning, pupils develop their understanding of phonics, pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar, enabling them to communicate with increasing confidence and accuracy.
We want pupils to become enthusiastic and resilient language learners who are willing to take risks, embrace challenges and understand that making mistakes is an important part of the learning process. Through language learning, pupils gain valuable cultural capital and develop the confidence and communication skills needed to thrive in an increasingly diverse and interconnected world.
Implementation
Spanish is taught weekly throughout Key Stage 2 using the Language Angels Scheme of Learning. The curriculum is carefully sequenced to ensure knowledge and skills build progressively from Year 3 to Year 6, enabling pupils to become increasingly confident, fluent and independent language learners.
Our curriculum is built around three key strands:
Phonics and Pronunciation
Pupils learn to recognise, reproduce and apply key Spanish sounds and phonetic patterns. This enables them to read unfamiliar words with increasing accuracy and develop confidence when speaking.
Vocabulary Development
High-frequency and relevant vocabulary is introduced systematically and revisited regularly. Through retrieval practice, pupils learn to recall vocabulary from memory and apply it successfully in new contexts.
Grammar and Sentence Structure
Pupils develop an understanding of how Spanish works. They learn grammatical concepts such as gender, articles, adjective agreement, verb forms and sentence structure, enabling them to move from single-word responses to increasingly complex phrases and sentences.
Across each unit, pupils develop skills in:
Lessons include songs, games, role-play, partner discussion, questioning, reading activities and independent writing opportunities. Teachers make meaningful cross-curricular links wherever possible.
Retrieval is central to our curriculum design. Previously taught vocabulary, phonics and grammar are regularly revisited to strengthen long-term memory and build secure foundations for future learning.
Assessment for learning is embedded throughout lessons. Teachers use questioning, observation, pupil discussion, written outcomes and end-of-unit assessments to identify misconceptions and inform future teaching.
Learning about Spain and the wider Spanish-speaking world is woven throughout the curriculum, helping pupils develop intercultural understanding and an appreciation of the rich diversity represented within our school community and beyond.

By the end of Key Stage 2, pupils demonstrate growing confidence, enthusiasm and fluency as language learners. They have secure foundations in Spanish and are able to apply their knowledge with increasing independence.
Most importantly, pupils leave Oak Gardens as confident, resilient and curious learners who understand the value of communication, cultural understanding and language learning. They are well prepared for the next stage of their education and equipped to continue their language-learning journey successfully.

Music
Intent
At Oak Gardens Primary School, we believe that music is a powerful and universal language that enriches children’s lives, nurtures creativity and supports personal development. Our ambition is for every child to develop a lifelong appreciation of music and to recognise its significance across different cultures, communities and traditions.
Through a rich and inclusive curriculum, pupils develop their skills as performers, composers and listeners whilst building a secure understanding of musical concepts and vocabulary. We aim to inspire children to express themselves creatively, explore their musical potential and develop the confidence to participate fully in musical experiences.
Music contributes significantly to our pupils’ wider development, fostering important life skills such as collaboration, communication, resilience, leadership and critical thinking. We believe all children should have access to high-quality musical opportunities regardless of their starting points and that every child should leave Oak Gardens Primary School with the confidence to see themselves as a musician.
Our curriculum celebrates diversity and promotes cultural understanding through exposure to a wide range of musical genres, traditions and influential musicians from around the world. Through this, children develop an appreciation of different cultures and gain the cultural capital needed to thrive in modern Britain and beyond.
Implementation
Our music curriculum is carefully sequenced to ensure pupils build knowledge, skills and understanding progressively throughout their primary education. We use Kapow Primary Music to support the delivery of a broad and balanced curriculum, providing clear progression in musical learning from Early Years through to Year 2.
In Key Stage 1, children develop their understanding of pulse, rhythm, pitch, tempo and dynamics through singing, listening, composing, movement and performance activities. They learn to express their ideas creatively whilst developing confidence and enjoyment in music-making.
In Key Stage 2, instrumental learning forms a significant part of our music provision. Pupils in Year 3 learn to play the xylophone, developing their understanding of notation, rhythm and melody. Pupils in Years 4, 5 and 6 learn to play the steel pans through specialist teaching, developing instrumental technique, ensemble performance skills, musical vocabulary and the discipline required to perform collaboratively.
Our renowned steel pan provision is a distinctive strength of music at Oak Gardens Primary School and has become an integral part of the school’s identity. As pupils progress through Years 4 to 6, they develop increasingly sophisticated instrumental and ensemble performance skills, enabling them to perform with confidence and musicality for a variety of audiences. The high standard of musicianship demonstrated by our pupils means that our steel pan groups are regularly sought after to perform at community celebrations, launch events and cultural festivals, including the Blackheath Kite Festival. These opportunities enable children to experience the excitement and responsibility of performing in public, helping to develop confidence, resilience, collaboration and a strong sense of achievement. Through these experiences, pupils gain valuable cultural capital, strengthen their connection with the local community and create lasting memories that enrich their primary school journey.
Singing is at the heart of our music curriculum. Pupils from Years 1 to 6 participate in regular whole-school singing sessions, developing vocal technique, musical memory, pitch accuracy and performance confidence whilst fostering a strong sense of belonging and community.
Our pupils also benefit from our valued partnership with Blackheath Halls, participating in collaborative music projects, workshops and mass singing events alongside children from other schools. These experiences give pupils opportunities to perform in larger ensembles, build confidence, receive high-quality musical tuition, and broaden their appreciation of the performing arts.
Performance opportunities are carefully planned throughout the year and form an integral part of our music curriculum. Children regularly perform to their peers, families and the wider community, celebrating their achievements and developing confidence as musicians. Our steel pan programme culminates in a vibrant end-of-year performance that showcases pupils’ musical progress and brings our school community together through celebration and shared experiences.
Through our listening curriculum, pupils explore music from a diverse range of cultures, traditions, genres and historical periods. In line with our commitment as a Race and Conscious Equality Silver Charter Mark, we ensure that the music children study reflects the rich diversity of our school community and the wider world. This enables pupils to see themselves represented within the curriculum whilst developing respect, understanding and appreciation for the experiences and contributions of others.
Impact
By the time pupils leave Oak Gardens Primary School, they have developed a strong foundation of musical knowledge, skills and understanding. They can perform with increasing confidence, compose creatively and listen critically, using appropriate musical vocabulary to discuss and evaluate music.
Pupils demonstrate enthusiasm for music and take pride in their performances. They understand how music connects people, cultures, and communities, and appreciate its role in promoting wellbeing, self-expression, and personal identity.
Through specialist instrumental tuition, collaborative music-making and high-profile performance opportunities, pupils develop confidence, resilience, discipline and a sense of responsibility. They learn how dedication and perseverance contribute to success and experience the pride that comes from achieving excellence as part of a team.
Our music curriculum equips children with the confidence to participate in musical opportunities both within and beyond school. Through high-quality teaching, specialist instrumental tuition and meaningful performance experiences, pupils leave Oak Gardens as confident, reflective and resilient young musicians who value music as an important part of their lives and the wider world.

At Oak Gardens Primary School, we believe that every child has the right to be safe, heard, valued and inspired to succeed. Art and Design
Intent
At the Phoenix Federation, we believe that Art and Design is an essential part of a broad, balanced and ambitious curriculum. Through art, pupils develop creativity, imagination, self-expression and the confidence to communicate their ideas, thoughts and experiences in meaningful and diverse ways.
Guided by the National Curriculum and informed by the AccessArt Primary Art Curriculum, we aim to nurture every child as an artist, designer and creative thinker. We provide rich opportunities for pupils to explore, experiment, take risks and develop their own artistic voice through a wide range of artistic disciplines, including drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking, collage, textiles, digital media and design.
Our curriculum is carefully sequenced to ensure children progressively develop their knowledge, skills and understanding of artistic processes, materials and techniques. We want pupils to understand that art is not simply about producing a final piece but about exploring ideas, revisiting concepts, reflecting upon work and learning from the creative journey.
We are committed to exposing children to a diverse range of artists, designers, craftspeople, architects and artistic movements from different cultures, backgrounds and periods of history. Through this, pupils gain a deeper appreciation of the rich contribution that art makes to society and develop respect for different perspectives, identities and forms of expression.
As a Federation, we believe that creativity plays a vital role in developing curiosity, resilience and innovation. We encourage our pupils to be aspirational in their ideas, brave when taking creative risks, compassionate towards the viewpoints and experiences of others, determined in refining their work and enlightened through engagement with artistic and cultural experiences.

Using the AccessArt curriculum as a framework, pupils engage in a creative journey that allows them to explore materials, develop techniques, investigate the work of artists and create increasingly sophisticated outcomes. Learning is sequenced to build upon prior knowledge and experiences, ensuring children continually develop their understanding and mastery of artistic concepts.
A central feature of our curriculum is the use of sketchbooks, which act as personal creative journals. Sketchbooks provide pupils with a safe space to investigate, experiment, record observations, generate ideas, practise techniques, evaluate outcomes and reflect on their artistic development. Assessment begins with consideration of prior learning and is ongoing throughout each unit. Teachers use observation, discussion, questioning, sketchbook reviews and pupil reflections to inform future learning. This ensures that teaching remains responsive and that all pupils make progress in their artistic understanding and technical skills.
We are committed to ensuring all children can access and succeed within the Art curriculum. Teaching is adapted appropriately to support pupils with SEND, disadvantaged pupils and those learning English as an Additional Language, whilst maintaining high expectations for all learners.
Learning is enriched through engagement with galleries, museums, cultural organisations, visiting artists and creative experiences. Wherever possible, pupils explore the artistic heritage of their local area alongside significant national and international artists, helping them understand how creativity can shape communities and influence the wider world.
Cross-curricular links are carefully considered, allowing pupils to apply their creativity and artistic understanding across a range of subjects while maintaining the distinct disciplinary knowledge of Art and Design.

pageCache.pageTitle: Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) - Oak Gardens Primary School
pageCache.text:
Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS)
At Oak Gardens Primary School, our Early Years Foundation Stage curriculum is inspired by the principles and values of the Reggio Emilia approach. We believe every child is a capable, curious, creative and competent learner. Through nurturing relationships, high expectations and meaningful learning experiences, we ensure that children’s interests, backgrounds, ideas and individual needs are at the heart of our provision.
Our ambitious and carefully sequenced curriculum is designed to provide all children with the knowledge, skills, vocabulary and experiences they need to succeed. Drawing upon the statutory EYFS framework, we provide a broad, balanced and inclusive curriculum across all seven areas of learning. The three prime areas, Communication and Language, Personal, Social and Emotional Development, and Physical Development, underpin all learning and create strong foundations for future success. Alongside these, children develop their understanding within the specific areas of Literacy, Mathematics, Understanding the World, and Expressive Arts and Design.
We recognise that language is fundamental to learning and future achievement. Therefore, communication, speech and language development are central to our curriculum design. Through high-quality interactions, purposeful questioning and rich learning experiences, adults explicitly develop children’s vocabulary, comprehension, speaking and listening skills. We believe every conversation matters and that every interaction offers an opportunity to extend language, deepen thinking, and support children’s understanding of the world around them. This is particularly important in ensuring equitable outcomes for children with SEND and those learning English as an Additional Language (EAL).
Our curriculum combines carefully planned themes and experiences with opportunities to follow children’s interests and curiosities. This balance ensures that children acquire important knowledge and skills whilst developing a genuine love of learning. Learning is meaningful, engaging and responsive, enabling children to make connections, revisit concepts and build increasingly sophisticated understanding over time.
Play is a fundamental vehicle for learning within our EYFS provision. Through purposeful play, children investigate, explore, create, collaborate and solve problems independently and with others. Our expertly designed learning environments act as a ‘third teacher’, providing stimulating opportunities that promote curiosity, critical thinking, communication and creativity. Carefully selected resources encourage children to take ownership of their learning, make choices and develop sustained engagement.
A key priority within our provision is the development of independence, resilience and positive learning behaviours. We support children to become confident learners who are willing to take risks, challenge themselves, persevere when faced with difficulty and celebrate their achievements. Through consistent routines, clear expectations and supportive relationships, children develop the confidence, self-regulation and self-belief required for lifelong learning.
Our indoor and outdoor learning environments are integral to our curriculum. Children benefit from daily opportunities to learn both inside and outside, developing their physical skills, creativity, social interaction, understanding of nature and problem-solving abilities. Outdoor learning provides rich opportunities to investigate, explore, collaborate and apply knowledge across all areas of learning in meaningful contexts.
Inclusion lies at the heart of everything we do. We recognise that every child enters school with unique experiences, strengths and starting points. Through careful assessment, responsive planning, and adaptive teaching, we ensure all children can access the curriculum successfully and achieve their full potential. Staff work closely with families and external agencies to identify needs, remove barriers and provide timely support where required.
Assessment is embedded within daily practice and is used to inform teaching and learning. Through observation, interaction and professional dialogue, practitioners develop a detailed understanding of what children know, understand and can do. This ongoing assessment enables staff to identify next steps, provide challenge, address misconceptions and ensure learning continually builds upon prior knowledge. Assessment is purposeful, responsive and focused on securing progress for every child.
We place great importance on developing children’s cultural capital by providing a wealth of experiences that broaden horizons, spark curiosity and deepen understanding of the world. Through visits, visitors, stories, exploration and memorable experiences, children develop the knowledge and confidence needed to engage with future learning and life beyond school.
By the end of EYFS, we aim for children to be confident communicators, independent learners, resilient problem-solvers and enthusiastic explorers. We strive to ensure every child leaves Reception with secure foundations across all areas of learning, a strong sense of self, positive attitudes towards learning and the knowledge, skills and confidence needed to flourish as they transition into Key Stage 1.
Intent
At Oak Gardens Primary School, our intent is to provide every child with a highly ambitious, language-rich and inclusive start to their educational journey. We are committed to developing confident, independent and resilient learners who are equipped with the knowledge, skills and attitudes required for future success. Through our Reggio Emilia-inspired approach, children learn in a stimulating environment where curiosity, creativity and exploration are valued and celebrated. We ensure all children, regardless of their starting points, have the opportunity to thrive, achieve, and develop a lifelong love of learning.
Implementation
Our curriculum is carefully sequenced to build knowledge and skills progressively across all seven areas of learning. High-quality interactions, explicit vocabulary teaching, purposeful play, direct teaching and meaningful first-hand experiences underpin our practice. Skilled practitioners continuously assess learning and adapt teaching to meet children’s needs, ensuring appropriate support and challenge for all learners. Indoor and outdoor environments are thoughtfully designed to promote independence, communication, critical thinking and exploration.
Impact
Children leave EYFS as confident, capable and enthusiastic learners who are ready for the challenges of Key Stage 1. They demonstrate strong communication skills, independence, positive learning behaviours and secure foundations across all areas of learning. Through our ambitious curriculum, children develop the knowledge, skills, vocabulary and cultural capital needed to succeed in their future education and wider life experiences.

English
At the Phoenix Federation, we believe that strong literacy skills are fundamental to children’s success across the curriculum and beyond. Our English curriculum aims to develop confident speakers, fluent and enthusiastic readers and purposeful, independent writers.
High-quality, diverse and language-rich texts are central to our approach. Through reading, writing and spoken language, children develop their vocabulary, deepen their knowledge and understanding of the world and learn to communicate confidently and effectively. Our curriculum is carefully sequenced so that new knowledge and skills build on what children have previously learned. Key knowledge and skills are explicitly taught, revisited, practised and applied so that children develop fluency, confidence and increasing independence.
Reading
Reading is at the heart of the Phoenix Federation, and we want all children to develop a genuine love of reading. Children have access to a wide range of high-quality, diverse and language-rich books and reading materials that reflect our community and the wider world. Every classroom has an inviting reading area, and children have regular opportunities to read independently, read with others and listen to adults reading aloud.
Our teaching develops both word reading and language comprehension. Children are taught to read accurately and fluently while developing the vocabulary, knowledge and comprehension skills needed to understand increasingly challenging texts.
In EYFS and KS1, children are taught phonics daily through Read Write Inc. (RWI). Children learn to hear, say, read and write sounds and use these to blend words for reading and segment words for spelling. Children who require further support continue to receive targeted phonics teaching beyond KS1 so that gaps in foundational reading knowledge are addressed quickly.
In KS2, children take part in a daily 45-minute reading session using the Destination Reader approach. Carefully selected, high-quality texts are explored as a whole class. Teachers explicitly model reading strategies before children practise and apply these with increasing independence. Children develop their ability to predict, clarify, question, summarise, make connections, evaluate, retrieve information and make inferences, using evidence from the text to explain and justify their thinking.
Alongside comprehension, we explicitly develop reading fluency. Teachers model fluent and expressive reading and provide opportunities for children to reread and practise texts, developing accuracy, automaticity, appropriate pace and expression. Children who are not yet reading fluently receive additional targeted teaching and practice.
Reading for pleasure is promoted throughout the Federation. Adults regularly read aloud, introducing children to a wide range of authors, genres and texts that they may not independently choose. Children are encouraged to talk about books, make recommendations, explore different authors and develop their own preferences and identities as readers. Children are also encouraged to read regularly at home and share their reading with an adult where appropriate.
By the end of KS1, children should be able to:
By the end of KS2, children should be able to:
decode unfamiliar words using their phonic knowledge
read fluently, accurately and confidently
understand and discuss increasingly challenging texts
retrieve information and make appropriate inferences
use strategies to understand unfamiliar vocabulary
Writing
At the Phoenix Federation, we want children to become confident, fluent and purposeful writers who can communicate their ideas clearly and effectively.
We use the Luminary scheme of writing as a key resource to support the teaching of writing. High-quality, diverse and language-rich texts provide meaningful contexts for writing and expose children to ambitious vocabulary, different voices, styles and text structures. Writing opportunities have a clear purpose, audience and context, with children writing to entertain, inform, explain, persuade and instruct. Where appropriate, children also apply and develop their writing across the wider curriculum.
Our approach recognises that successful writing depends on children developing both transcription – spelling and handwriting – and composition – generating, organising and communicating ideas. These skills are explicitly taught and carefully sequenced so that children become increasingly fluent and independent writers.
The foundations for writing begin in EYFS. Children develop their spoken language and learn to compose ideas orally alongside the systematic teaching of phonics, spelling and handwriting. Children are encouraged to say and rehearse what they want to write before recording their ideas. As transcription skills become more secure, children are increasingly able to focus their attention on the content and composition of their writing.
Spoken language continues to play an important role throughout the writing process. Children discuss ideas, explore vocabulary and rehearse sentences orally before writing. Teachers explicitly model how writers generate and organise ideas, construct and combine sentences, draft, reread, revise, edit and evaluate their work. Shared and guided writing provide opportunities for children to practise these processes with support before scaffolds are gradually reduced and children take increasing responsibility for their own writing.
Children are taught that revising and editing are different processes. Revising focuses on improving meaning, vocabulary, sentence construction and organisation, while editing focuses on improving accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar.
We value quality over quantity. Children are supported to secure strong foundations in spelling, handwriting and sentence construction before being expected to produce increasingly sustained and complex pieces of writing.
Phonics and Spelling
In EYFS and Year 1, children receive daily systematic synthetic phonics teaching through Read Write Inc. Phonics supports both early reading and spelling by teaching children the relationship between sounds and letters.
As children progress, spelling is taught explicitly and systematically in line with the National Curriculum. Children develop their understanding of age-appropriate spelling patterns, rules and word structures and are given regular opportunities to practise and apply these within their writing. Dictation is used where appropriate to support children in applying their phonics, spelling, punctuation and sentence knowledge.
Teachers use assessment to identify gaps in spelling knowledge and provide additional teaching and practice where required. Our aim is for spelling to become increasingly accurate and automatic so that children can focus more fully on what they want to communicate.
Sentence Construction, Grammar and Punctuation
Effective sentence construction is fundamental to successful writing. Children are explicitly taught how to construct, combine and manipulate sentences to communicate their ideas clearly. Teachers model sentence construction and provide opportunities for children to orally rehearse, practise and improve sentences before applying their learning independently.
Grammar and punctuation are taught explicitly and purposefully. Children learn the grammatical knowledge and terminology outlined in the National Curriculum and, importantly, how this knowledge can help them control sentences and convey meaning.
Wherever possible, grammar and punctuation are explored through meaningful contexts, including the high-quality texts children read, sentence-level work, shared writing and children’s own writing. Our aim is for children to understand how and why writers make grammatical and punctuation choices rather than simply learning rules in isolation.
Handwriting
Handwriting is taught explicitly and progressively across the Phoenix Federation using the Letter-Join Programme. From Reception, children develop the physical skills, pencil control and accurate letter formation needed for writing. As they progress, children are taught appropriate letter joins and work towards handwriting that is fluent, legible and increasingly automatic.
Children practise handwriting regularly, and adults consistently model high-quality handwriting. Developing fluent handwriting is an important part of becoming an effective writer, as increasing automaticity enables children to focus more of their attention on the content and composition of their writing.
Spoken Language and Vocabulary
Spoken language underpins reading and writing. Children have regular opportunities to develop their confidence in speaking, listening and communicating their ideas clearly. They learn to listen and respond to others, explain their thinking, ask questions, develop ideas through discussion and adapt their spoken language for different audiences and purposes.
Partner and group discussion, oral rehearsal, storytelling, drama, debate, presentations and performances provide purposeful opportunities for children to develop their spoken language. Teachers model high-quality talk and support children to articulate increasingly complex ideas.
Developing a rich vocabulary is central to this work. Through high-quality texts, purposeful discussion and explicit teaching, children encounter and explore new vocabulary in meaningful contexts. Teachers explicitly teach the meaning and use of new words and provide repeated opportunities for children to hear, say, read and use them. Children are encouraged to be curious about language, make connections between words and select vocabulary carefully when speaking and writing.
Assessment and Inclusion
Our English curriculum is ambitious for all children, including those with SEND, disadvantaged pupils and children learning English as an additional language. Teachers maintain high expectations while making appropriate adaptations so that children can access and succeed within the curriculum.
Assessment is an integral part of teaching. Teachers use ongoing assessment during lessons, children’s independent work and appropriate statutory and school-based assessments to identify what children know, what they can apply independently and where further teaching or practice is required.
Children who are at risk of falling behind are identified as early as possible. Targeted teaching and additional practice focus precisely on the foundational knowledge and skills that have not yet been secured. This may include additional phonics teaching, reading fluency practice, vocabulary and language development, spelling and handwriting practice, oral rehearsal, sentence construction or targeted support with comprehension and composition.
For children learning English as an additional language, particular attention is given to developing vocabulary, high-quality talk, modelling and providing repeated opportunities to hear and use language. For children with SEND, teaching is appropriately adapted while maintaining ambitious curriculum goals.
Where children have gaps in foundational knowledge, these are addressed rather than moving children on to increasingly complex learning before they are ready. The impact of additional support is reviewed regularly and teaching is adapted accordingly.
English leaders work alongside teachers to ensure that the curriculum is implemented consistently and effectively across the Federation. Monitoring, professional development and ongoing support are used to strengthen subject knowledge, identify priorities and continually improve provision.
Our aim is for every child to leave the Phoenix Federation as an enthusiastic reader, effective writer and confident communicator, equipped with the literacy knowledge and skills they need for the next stage of their education and beyond.
